list.listitem: DEET-containing repellents offer the most protection from insect bites. A
Insecticide-treated clothing and bed nets reduce insect bites. A
Patients with prior severe systemic reactions to insect bites/stings should carry self-injectable epinephrine. C
Although most bites and stings cause local inflammation that gradually resolves without treatment, systemic allergic responses may occur. C
Venom immunotherapy significantly reduces the risk of severe systemic sting reactions in patients with a prior history of such reactions. A

background.definition: The bites and stings of insects and spiders produce a transient local inflammatory reaction characterized by pain, redness, and swelling at the site of the punctured skin. Allergies to components of their venom can produce mild systemic reactions or severe, even fatal, anaphylactic reactions.

list.listitem: Mosquitoes alone spread infections, such as malaria, dengue, Zika, and West Nile virus, to more than 700 million people annually.
Up to 3% of adults experience life-threatening systemic reactions to insect stings.
Stinging insects of the Hymenoptera order probably cause more deaths than any other venomous animal.
Mosquitoes are a common and important cause of insect bites worldwide.
Insect bites are also inflicted by biting flies (horse and deer flies), fleas, and ticks.
The Hymenoptera order of insects—including yellow jackets, wasps, bees, and ants—inflict stings and may cause systemic allergic reactions.
Spiders use fangs to bite and inject poison.
Concentrated irritant substances are injected during bites and stings, causing local inflammation.
Individuals can produce a cell-mediated immune response and develop IgE antibodies to insect venom, putting them at higher risk for systemic reactions to insect stings.
The toxins injected by the brown recluse spider, including hyaluronidase and sphingomyelinase-D, can cause necrotic skin ulcers and systemic symptoms.
Individuals should avoid times and locations of greatest insect activity. C
DEET-containing repellents offer the most protection from insect bites. A
Permethrin-treated fabric reduces insect bites. A
Patients with prior severe systemic reactions should carry self-injectable epinephrine. C

DEET-containing compounds are the most effective mosquito repellents; higher concentrations of DEET provide longer-lasting protection. DEET repellents also protect against ticks, fleas, and biting flies.
Repellents containing higher concentrations (20%) of picaridin (also known as icaridin) demonstrate similar efficacy to DEET, and picaridin may be better tolerated than DEET.
Soybean oil-based mosquito repellents and oil of lemon eucalyptus provide protection equal to that of a low-concentration DEET product.
DEET-impregnated wristbands and electronic mosquito repellents do not prevent bites.
Applying 0.5% permethrin to tent fabric and clothing reduces mosquito and tick bites.
Use of insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) in malaria-endemic regions of Africa helps prevent malaria transmission.
Use of ITNs by pregnant women in malaria-endemic regions of Africa reduced placental malaria, low birth weight, and fetal loss.
No repellents deter stinging insects, like wasps, bees, and ants.
People who are allergic to stings should be cautious during outdoor activities and yard work.

CDC recommends that pregnant women should not travel to areas with active Zika outbreaks and should use condoms if their sex partner has traveled to one of these areas. Pregnant women living in endemic areas should take strong steps to avoid mosquito bites, such as living in an air-conditioned environment without open windows, use of mosquito nets, protective clothing, and DEET.
Physicians should prescribe self-injectable epinephrine (0.3 mg or 0.3 mL of 1:1,000 dilution) to patients with a history of systemic reactions to stings.
Insect and spider bites and stings cause local pain, redness, and swelling, and may induce a systemic allergic response. C
Individuals with a history of systemic reactions to insect stings should undergo specific skin or serum testing to be considered for immunotherapy. A

Insect bites usually cause a temporary local inflammatory reaction with pain, itching, redness, and swelling at the site of the bite. Insect stings cause a similar but more painful local erythematous wheal, and may cause a larger local reaction with swelling that lasts for a week.

Stings can also cause systemic allergic reactions in individuals who produced IgE antibodies during previous exposure. Systemic reactions vary in severity but may include urticaria, bronchospasm, throat swelling, hypotension, and shock.
Most spider bites are painless or cause a red, tender nodule with fang puncture markings. Capture of the spider after a bite helps with diagnosis.
Some spiders, such as the brown recluse, frequently cause necrotic, slowly healing ulcers, typically on the extremities.

Other insect bites or skin infections are commonly misdiagnosed as spider bites. Always consider community-acquired MRSA in patients presenting with report of "spider bite" or any necrotic skin lesion.
Skin testing with insect venoms should be performed on patients who have experienced systemic reactions to stings and may be candidates for immunotherapy.
Skin testing is the most sensitive (93%) method to identify patients who are allergic to bee or wasp venom.
Detection of allergen-specific IgE antibodies in serum by the radioallergosorbent test (RAST) is less sensitive than skin tests, but may be useful when skin tests cannot be performed.
The basophil activation test is less sensitive (88%) than skin testing, but has better specificity than immunoassays for specific IgE antibodies.
The degree of sensitivity on testing does not reliably predict the severity of sting reactions.
Patients with typical, transient, local reactions to insect and spider bites and stings will not usually present to a physician because the reactions generally resolve without treatment.
If the patient seeks care for a skin lesion or an allergic reaction, always ask whether an insect or spider bite or sting was witnessed; the insect or spider should be identified, if possible.
Always consider community-acquired MRSA in patients presenting with report of "spider bite" or any necrotic skin lesion.
Ascertain whether a local or systemic reaction occurred. If a severe systemic reaction occurred, refer the patient to an allergist/immunologist for testing and possible immunotherapy.
No treatment is usually required for local reactions to insect and spider bites and stings. C
Venom immunotherapy significantly reduces the risk of subsequent systemic allergic reactions to insect stings. A
Oral antihistamines reduce the swelling and itching caused by bites.
Anaphylaxis from stings should be treated according to emergency protocols, including the administration of intramuscular epinephrine (0.3-0.5 mL of 1:1000 dilution).

Venom immunotherapy should be offered to patients who have had a systemic reaction to an insect sting and have a positive skin test result or elevated levels of venom-specific IgE. It prevents sting anaphylaxis in 75% to 98% of patients and improves patients' perceived quality of life. Venom immunotherapy should be continued for at least 3 to 5 years but may need to be continued indefinitely.

Physicians should prescribe self-injectable epinephrine to patients with a history of systemic reactions to stings. The dose is 0.3 mg for individuals weighing more than 66 pounds, and 0.15 mg for patients 65 pounds and lighter.
No known treatments shorten healing time or reduce scarring in suspected brown recluse spider bites. Antibiotics are not indicated except to treat secondary infection.
Tetanus prophylaxis is recommended after a spider bite.
A homeopathic after-bite gel reduced the redness but not itching of mosquito bites.
Cold compresses may decrease local swelling and pain.
Immediate removal of the stinger from the skin decreases the swelling of bee stings.

Individuals with moderate to severe systemic reactions need to be hospitalized because of potential respiratory and cardiovascular compromise, including edema of the pharynx, bronchoconstriction, and hypotension.
Insects and spiders usually produce a local inflammatory reaction that gradually resolves within a few days. C
Of those individuals with a history of insect-sting anaphylaxis, 28% develop a second anaphylactic reaction with a sting challenge.
Stay indoors between dusk and dawn to avoid mosquito bites.
Wear light-colored clothing with long sleeves and long pants tucked into socks.
Do not apply perfume or use scented soap, shampoo, or lotion.
Use enough repellent to lightly cover exposed skin and clothing.
Spray permethrin onto clothes and hiking/camping gear.
Wash with soap and water when the repellent is no longer needed.
Check your body for ticks and shower or bathe within 2 hours of returning from tick habitat.
Allergic individuals should avoid bushes, garbage cans, and picnic areas.
Those with prior serious systemic reactions should carry an emergency epinephrine pen.
DEET-containing products are safe for pregnant and lactating women.
Do not start venom immunotherapy during pregnancy.
Repellents containing 10% to 30% DEET appear to be safe for children older than 2 months.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends applying DEET-containing products not more than once per day to children.
